newsitem.title: CHINA: Boeing says about 30 killed in China crash.
newsitem.headline: Boeing says about 30 killed in China crash.

text.p: About 30 people were killed in China's first aviation disaster for almost three years when a Boeing 737 on a domestic flight crashed while landing in the southern city of Shenzhen, a Boeing Co spokesman said on Friday.

China Southern Airlines flight CZ3456 from the southwestern city of Chongqing crashed during a thunderstorm at the new Huangtian airport serving Shenzhen, a prosperous town on the Chinese border with Hong Kong, local officials said.
The flight had originally been scheduled to land at Shenzhen's international airport but had been diverted because of the heavy rain.
A Boeing spokesman in Beijing said it appeared around 30 people were killed when the three-year-old 737-300 crashed and burned at around 9.30 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Thursday night.
"The unconfirmed figure we have now is 30," the spokesman said by telephone, adding that little other information on the accident was available.
"It's pretty chaotic out there," he said.
Officials in Shenzhen declined to confirm the death toll, but said at least 10 of the 65 passengers and nine crew aboard the airliner were killed after it broke up and burst into flames.
The official Xinhua news agency described casualties as heavy, but gave no death toll.
"The fuselage of the airliner was broken," Xinhua said. "The cause of the accident is still under investigation."
A group of Thai tourists were aboard the aircraft, an airline spokesman said. It was not immediately known how many were in the group or if any of them were among the dead.
Staff at one Shenzhen hospital said two middle-aged Thai men had been injured but that their condition was not serious.
The Hong Kong Standard quoted a spokesman for Shenzhen's People's Hospital as saying one Thai woman was admitted with multiple fractures of her knees, ribs and head, but her condition was stable.
"The attitude of the plane during landing was wrong," one airline official said by telephone after the crash, which happened as Shenzhen was being pelted with rain from a severe thunderstorm.
The airliner's co-pilot was among those killed by the impact or by the blaze that tore through the airliner immediately afterwards, said another official.

The disaster was the first to hit China Southern since another of its fleet of about 35 Boeing 737s slammed into a hill near the scenic southern city of Guilin in November, 1992. That accident killed all 141 people aboard.

Chinese aviation officials had been celebrating almost three years without a serious accident, a record credited to improved precautions taken after a Russian-made Tupolev-154 exploded in mid-air after takeoff on a domestic flight in June, 1994.
That disaster killed 160 people, making it the worst reported accident in China's aviation history.

It occurred just months after the International Airline Passengers Association cited China as one of the most dangerous places in the world to fly after five aircraft crashed in 1993 and 10 airliners were hijacked to Taiwan.
In 1992, a series of accidents over a four-month period killed 276 passengers, including many foreigners.
